compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
Running a community charity market, either may volunteer: one checks the application and follows up on approvals, the other writes the copy and talks to stallholders until closing. Outsiders see two committed people, and behaviour alone does not reveal the letters.

The resemblance comes mostly from the situation and the duty, not from shared letters — this pair shares none. In the same event, under the same approval rules, two people in similar posts behave more alike than their types would suggest; change the post and the same person changes too.

The difference sits on four axes. Sourcing: trusting checkable paperwork and precedent, or seeing faster the pattern and possibility those materials point at. Basis for judgement: whether one standard applies consistently, or what this means for specific people. Outward stance: settling the arrangement, or keeping room. Direction: energy going to what is being pushed forward outside, or returning first to one's own judgement. Each axis stands on its own and none substitutes for another — in particular, do not read "weighs standards" as "does not care about people", or "weighs how people feel" as "has no standards".

### Material returned: fill the gaps first, or question the plan

In a fictional community market application, the reviewer asks for a clearer description of the temporary power supply. Both organisers see the same note, have the same authority and face the same deadline.

One response breaks the note into checkable questions: is what is missing the wiring diagram, the electrician's certificate, or the load figures? Call the office, ask which field exactly, complete the list, and run the same check over similar material. The basis is that requirements can be checked item by item, and once complete the application can proceed.

The other response returns to the plan itself: the electrical supply was requested in order to add a sound system — is the sound system necessary? Could a quieter event serve the same purpose? Would it reduce disruption for neighbours? The organisers would still confirm the applicable requirements with the reviewer. The basis is what this arrangement means for the people present.

Either response can appear and either can be used; the difference is the basis, not who moves first. Anyone carrying a safety duty, of any type, will ask about the hard conditions first; with half a day left, anyone of any type may fill the fields that can be filled. Filling and thinking can also be combined: ask which fields are mandatory, then decide what can be cut.

The costs are clear on both sides. Filling without thinking may keep adding, until the event becomes a full sound-and-light production unrelated to the original idea; thinking without filling may reach the day before the deadline with every missing item still missing.

Keep the counterexamples. INFP will visit the office three times for one safety condition, and can write the remediation note in more detail than anyone; ESTJ will cut the sound system because "this part is unfriendly to nearby residents", then go back and complete the material. Experience, duty and authority all rewrite the approach; a single reaction cannot define a person.

A workable check: each writes a list of "must be satisfied" items and notes the basis after each — a hard approval requirement, a safety floor, an event goal, a personal preference. Then compare the facts and constraints first (which item is mandatory, who holds approval, when the deadline is), and only then discuss reasons and trade-offs. Two lists overlapping does not mean the disagreement is only about wording; not overlapping does not mean the goals differ: one may list an item as required by regulation, the other list the same item as required by the budget.

Line the two writings up: ESTJ is Te–Si–Ne–Fi and INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te. Read INFP's arrangement backwards and you get ESTJ's: dominant and inferior swap, auxiliary and third swap, and no part is missing.

A position describes a theoretical preference in type dynamics, not a scale of ability, not how effortful something feels, and not a sequence of actions. The same person shifts toward the other side when authorised, pressed with questions or asked to sign; under time pressure, ESTJ may hesitate over one detail and INFP may fill in the whole form in one go.

On the third position, ESTJ's Ne and INFP's Si are marked with different attitudes across sources, and some tables give only the function name. This page uses the common marking; when a version disagrees, check which table it cites, then return to the first two positions for this pair. compare_blocks.body:
Scope note: the two passages below are editorial fictions covering communication, the organisation of information and cost arrangements only, not approval outcomes, fire or electrical judgements; such judgements belong to the competent authority and licensed professionals.

Working together, the two easily get stuck when one is already at the office window and the other is still asking whether the thing should be done this way. It is rarely about who is right, but about which kind of information each handles first; writing the two lines separately is more useful than arguing.

### One market: coordinating approvals and working with stallholders

(Fictional scene.) The site is a patch of open ground outside a residential compound, and the organisers have been asked to confirm venue, fire-safety, noise and insurance requirements for this fictional event.

One approach works backwards: which stamp is needed by which date, who goes, missing items flagged in red, contacts saved to speed dial, and a visit in person when something sticks. The other talks to stallholders first: who will come, what they sell, whether anyone depends on this market for a month of groceries, and sets the scale from that.

Each has a blind spot. Focusing only on approvals can leave an event that meets the requirements but attracts few stalls or visitors; intentions alone may reach the day and find the power insufficient and the access route non-compliant.

The division follows experience, authority and willingness, not type: whoever knows the registration process, whoever knows the stallholders, whoever has time this week leads that line, and both lines need someone to sign off. Hard conditions — fire access, the load limit, the noise window — are confirmed with the authority by both together and written into one sheet; what can be adjusted, such as the number of stalls, the length of the performance, whether there is sound, is left to the content side. If neither knows the process, contact the relevant authority together, or ask someone experienced to walk the first round with you.

Once a week, ask whether anything that should not have been changed was changed in order to pass review, and put the answer in the minutes; only then does anyone remember what the original was.

### A shared flat's bills: how to handle a gap in the records

(Fictional scene.) Three flatmates share a flat, and after three months the expense records show a difference of 180 yuan.

One position pulls the transactions first and checks them one by one: who bought what, is there a receipt, how much per head; and proposes a fixed monthly transfer date, with reporting any expense over 50 yuan in the group chat. The other handles the cost of the conversation first: is it worth digging through three months of history for a hundred and something, shall we cover it this time and talk it through, while also remembering how awkward it felt to be audited.

Either position can be raised by anyone and accepted by anyone. Checking only the accounts easily turns living together into an audit; covering only the money leaves a new discrepancy next month and a layer of resentment in whoever pays.

The counterexamples are clear: INFP will propose a spreadsheet the second time it does not add up and get the rule established; ESTJ will say "let it go this time, you helped me move".

One method worth trying: agree on a threshold for recording shared expenses, such as 50 yuan in this example, and write down who carries what below it — absorbed individually, or pooled and split at month end. Without that, a shrinking difference in the records does not show the split is fairer, only that some spending has moved out of the records. After a trial month, review two things together: how much shared spending never entered the accounts, and whether each person feels the split was fair.

The resemblance comes mostly from the situation and the duty, not from shared letters — this pair shares none. In the same event, under the same approval rules, two people in similar posts behave more alike than their types would suggest; change the post and the same person changes too.

The difference sits on four axes. Sourcing: trusting checkable paperwork and precedent, or seeing faster the pattern and possibility those materials point at. Basis for judgement: whether one standard applies consistently, or what this means for specific people. Outward stance: settling the arrangement, or keeping room. Direction: energy going to what is being pushed forward outside, or returning first to one's own judgement. Each axis stands on its own and none substitutes for another — in particular, do not read "weighs standards" as "does not care about people", or "weighs how people feel" as "has no standards".
### Material returned: fill the gaps first, or question the plan

In a fictional community market application, the reviewer asks for a clearer description of the temporary power supply. Both organisers see the same note, have the same authority and face the same deadline.

One response breaks the note into checkable questions: is what is missing the wiring diagram, the electrician's certificate, or the load figures? Call the office, ask which field exactly, complete the list, and run the same check over similar material. The basis is that requirements can be checked item by item, and once complete the application can proceed.

The other response returns to the plan itself: the electrical supply was requested in order to add a sound system — is the sound system necessary? Could a quieter event serve the same purpose? Would it reduce disruption for neighbours? The organisers would still confirm the applicable requirements with the reviewer. The basis is what this arrangement means for the people present.

Either response can appear and either can be used; the difference is the basis, not who moves first. Anyone carrying a safety duty, of any type, will ask about the hard conditions first; with half a day left, anyone of any type may fill the fields that can be filled. Filling and thinking can also be combined: ask which fields are mandatory, then decide what can be cut.

The costs are clear on both sides. Filling without thinking may keep adding, until the event becomes a full sound-and-light production unrelated to the original idea; thinking without filling may reach the day before the deadline with every missing item still missing.

Keep the counterexamples. INFP will visit the office three times for one safety condition, and can write the remediation note in more detail than anyone; ESTJ will cut the sound system because "this part is unfriendly to nearby residents", then go back and complete the material. Experience, duty and authority all rewrite the approach; a single reaction cannot define a person.

A workable check: each writes a list of "must be satisfied" items and notes the basis after each — a hard approval requirement, a safety floor, an event goal, a personal preference. Then compare the facts and constraints first (which item is mandatory, who holds approval, when the deadline is), and only then discuss reasons and trade-offs. Two lists overlapping does not mean the disagreement is only about wording; not overlapping does not mean the goals differ: one may list an item as required by regulation, the other list the same item as required by the budget.

Line the two writings up: ESTJ is Te–Si–Ne–Fi and INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te. Read INFP's arrangement backwards and you get ESTJ's: dominant and inferior swap, auxiliary and third swap, and no part is missing.

It is rarely about who is right, but about which kind of information each handles first; writing the two lines separately is more useful than arguing.
### One market: coordinating approvals and working with stallholders

(Fictional scene.) The site is a patch of open ground outside a residential compound, and the organisers have been asked to confirm venue, fire-safety, noise and insurance requirements for this fictional event.

One approach works backwards: which stamp is needed by which date, who goes, missing items flagged in red, contacts saved to speed dial, and a visit in person when something sticks. The other talks to stallholders first: who will come, what they sell, whether anyone depends on this market for a month of groceries, and sets the scale from that.

Each has a blind spot. Focusing only on approvals can leave an event that meets the requirements but attracts few stalls or visitors; intentions alone may reach the day and find the power insufficient and the access route non-compliant.

The division follows experience, authority and willingness, not type: whoever knows the registration process, whoever knows the stallholders, whoever has time this week leads that line, and both lines need someone to sign off. Hard conditions — fire access, the load limit, the noise window — are confirmed with the authority by both together and written into one sheet; what can be adjusted, such as the number of stalls, the length of the performance, whether there is sound, is left to the content side. If neither knows the process, contact the relevant authority together, or ask someone experienced to walk the first round with you.
Once a week, ask whether anything that should not have been changed was changed in order to pass review, and put the answer in the minutes; only then does anyone remember what the original was.
### A shared flat's bills: how to handle a gap in the records
(Fictional scene.) Three flatmates share a flat, and after three months the expense records show a difference of 180 yuan.

One position pulls the transactions first and checks them one by one: who bought what, is there a receipt, how much per head; and proposes a fixed monthly transfer date, with reporting any expense over 50 yuan in the group chat. The other handles the cost of the conversation first: is it worth digging through three months of history for a hundred and something, shall we cover it this time and talk it through, while also remembering how awkward it felt to be audited.

Either position can be raised by anyone and accepted by anyone. Checking only the accounts easily turns living together into an audit; covering only the money leaves a new discrepancy next month and a layer of resentment in whoever pays.
The counterexamples are clear: INFP will propose a spreadsheet the second time it does not add up and get the rule established; ESTJ will say "let it go this time, you helped me move".

One method worth trying: agree on a threshold for recording shared expenses, such as 50 yuan in this example, and write down who carries what below it — absorbed individually, or pooled and split at month end. Without that, a shrinking difference in the records does not show the split is fairer, only that some spending has moved out of the records. After a trial month, review two things together: how much shared spending never entered the accounts, and whether each person feels the split was fair.

body: Do not read drive as dominance. Chasing progress is often because everyone knows it will not happen otherwise, and the same person may not raise their voice at home; conversely, a gentle speaker may not yield an inch on a deadline.

Do not read hesitation as having no view. Hesitation is often checking whether this fits one's own judgement, not waiting for someone else to decide. Once settled, it may be explained clearly or not explained again; how far someone holds depends on how much the matter matters to them, not on four letters.

Nor judge by "can they get things done". Navigating an application process and writing event copy are both skills, and both can be trained; a preference says only which end is cared about first, not what level can be reached.

One more to avoid: do not read "all four axes differ" as "complete opposites". The difference on an axis is one of emphasis, not one side having something the other lacks; both types check facts, consider people, make arrangements and keep room.

body: When you keep landing between ESTJ and INFP, check the instrument, version, language and how each axis score is defined, then which kind of situation you were referring to when answering: liaison, approvals, writing or support work may give you different examples to think about. No. That sentence presses four axes into one and turns two people into opposites.

Read by the four axes: E/I is whether attention and energy turn outward or inward more often; S/N whether sourcing weighs checkable facts and precedent or pattern and possibility; T/F whether judgement weighs one consistently applicable standard or what it means for specific people; J/P whether an arrangement is formed outward first or room is kept. items.question: Is the difference really just "one talks process, one talks feelings"?

items.answer:
Because whether two people can work together does not depend on how function labels are arranged. "Exactly reversed" is a description under the common four-function notation used here, not a cause of collaboration going well or badly.

Collaboration depends on clear duties, sufficient authority, shared information and aligned goals. In the same project both types may watch the process, and both may watch whether the thing is worth doing; the division is negotiated by experience and authority, not by function positions. Conversely, two people of the same type collaborating badly need no function arrangement to explain it.
items.question: With the function order fully reversed, how can they still work together?

items.answer:
Both types can chase a process, and both can adjust a plan for a value; a function position does not restrict what anyone can do.

The same behaviour cannot be read backwards into a function position. The same person behaves differently under different duties, authority and information, and later wording cannot identify which position was called on — lines such as "this is not about you" or "next time we follow the process" reflect the situation and relational pressure. What discriminates better is the reason: across comparable situations, do you more often cite "which requirement must be met, who is responsible", or "what this means for the people involved".
items.question: INFP also chases a process, and ESTJ also changes a plan for a feeling — how does that fit?

items.answer:
Not by type, but by experience, authority and willingness.

Both can ask about the hard conditions, and both can set the scale and the content. body: Running a community charity market, either may volunteer: one checks the application and follows up on approvals, the other writes the copy and talks to stallholders until closing. Outsiders see two committed people, and behaviour alone does not reveal the letters.

The resemblance comes mostly from the situation and the duty, not from shared letters — this pair shares none. In the same event, under the same approval rules, two people in similar posts behave more alike than their types would suggest; change the post and the same person changes too.

The difference sits on four axes. Sourcing: trusting checkable paperwork and precedent, or seeing faster the pattern and possibility those materials point at. Basis for judgement: whether one standard applies consistently, or what this means for specific people. Outward stance: settling the arrangement, or keeping room. Direction: energy going to what is being pushed forward outside, or returning first to one's own judgement. Each axis stands on its own and none substitutes for another — in particular, do not read "weighs standards" as "does not care about people", or "weighs how people feel" as "has no standards".
### Material returned: fill the gaps first, or question the plan

In a fictional community market application, the reviewer asks for a clearer description of the temporary power supply. Both organisers see the same note, have the same authority and face the same deadline.

One response breaks the note into checkable questions: is what is missing the wiring diagram, the electrician's certificate, or the load figures? Call the office, ask which field exactly, complete the list, and run the same check over similar material. The basis is that requirements can be checked item by item, and once complete the application can proceed.

The other response returns to the plan itself: the electrical supply was requested in order to add a sound system — is the sound system necessary? Could a quieter event serve the same purpose? Would it reduce disruption for neighbours? The organisers would still confirm the applicable requirements with the reviewer. The basis is what this arrangement means for the people present.

Either response can appear and either can be used; the difference is the basis, not who moves first. Anyone carrying a safety duty, of any type, will ask about the hard conditions first; with half a day left, anyone of any type may fill the fields that can be filled. Filling and thinking can also be combined: ask which fields are mandatory, then decide what can be cut.

The costs are clear on both sides. Filling without thinking may keep adding, until the event becomes a full sound-and-light production unrelated to the original idea; thinking without filling may reach the day before the deadline with every missing item still missing.

Keep the counterexamples. INFP will visit the office three times for one safety condition, and can write the remediation note in more detail than anyone; ESTJ will cut the sound system because "this part is unfriendly to nearby residents", then go back and complete the material. Experience, duty and authority all rewrite the approach; a single reaction cannot define a person.

A workable check: each writes a list of "must be satisfied" items and notes the basis after each — a hard approval requirement, a safety floor, an event goal, a personal preference. Then compare the facts and constraints first (which item is mandatory, who holds approval, when the deadline is), and only then discuss reasons and trade-offs. Two lists overlapping does not mean the disagreement is only about wording; not overlapping does not mean the goals differ: one may list an item as required by regulation, the other list the same item as required by the budget.
### Four identical parts, one fully reversed order

Line the two writings up: ESTJ is Te–Si–Ne–Fi and INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te. Read INFP's arrangement backwards and you get ESTJ's: dominant and inferior swap, auxiliary and third swap, and no part is missing.

A position describes a theoretical preference in type dynamics, not a scale of ability, not how effortful something feels, and not a sequence of actions. The same person shifts toward the other side when authorised, pressed with questions or asked to sign; under time pressure, ESTJ may hesitate over one detail and INFP may fill in the whole form in one go.

On the third position, ESTJ's Ne and INFP's Si are marked with different attitudes across sources, and some tables give only the function name. This page uses the common marking; when a version disagrees, check which table it cites, then return to the first two positions for this pair. The disagreement does not change the first two and does not explain how early anyone acts. Both full pages are the [ESTJ profile](/en/personality/estj) and the [INFP profile](/en/personality/infp).

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Running a community charity market, either may volunteer: one checks the application and follows up on approvals, the other writes the copy and talks to stallholders until closing. Outsiders see two committed people, and behaviour alone does not reveal the letters.

The resemblance comes mostly from the situation and the duty, not from shared letters — this pair shares none. In the same event, under the same approval rules, two people in similar posts behave more alike than their types would suggest; change the post and the same person changes too.

The difference sits on four axes. Sourcing: trusting checkable paperwork and precedent, or seeing faster the pattern and possibility those materials point at. Basis for judgement: whether one standard applies consistently, or what this means for specific people. Outward stance: settling the arrangement, or keeping room. Direction: energy going to what is being pushed forward outside, or returning first to one's own judgement. Each axis stands on its own and none substitutes for another — in particular, do not read "weighs standards" as "does not care about people", or "weighs how people feel" as "has no standards".

### Material returned: fill the gaps first, or question the plan

In a fictional community market application, the reviewer asks for a clearer description of the temporary power supply. Both organisers see the same note, have the same authority and face the same deadline.

One response breaks the note into checkable questions: is what is missing the wiring diagram, the electrician's certificate, or the load figures? Call the office, ask which field exactly, complete the list, and run the same check over similar material. The basis is that requirements can be checked item by item, and once complete the application can proceed.

The other response returns to the plan itself: the electrical supply was requested in order to add a sound system — is the sound system necessary? Could a quieter event serve the same purpose? Would it reduce disruption for neighbours? The organisers would still confirm the applicable requirements with the reviewer. The basis is what this arrangement means for the people present.

Either response can appear and either can be used; the difference is the basis, not who moves first. Anyone carrying a safety duty, of any type, will ask about the hard conditions first; with half a day left, anyone of any type may fill the fields that can be filled. Filling and thinking can also be combined: ask which fields are mandatory, then decide what can be cut.

The costs are clear on both sides. Filling without thinking may keep adding, until the event becomes a full sound-and-light production unrelated to the original idea; thinking without filling may reach the day before the deadline with every missing item still missing.

Keep the counterexamples. INFP will visit the office three times for one safety condition, and can write the remediation note in more detail than anyone; ESTJ will cut the sound system because "this part is unfriendly to nearby residents", then go back and complete the material. Experience, duty and authority all rewrite the approach; a single reaction cannot define a person.

A workable check: each writes a list of "must be satisfied" items and notes the basis after each — a hard approval requirement, a safety floor, an event goal, a personal preference. Then compare the facts and constraints first (which item is mandatory, who holds approval, when the deadline is), and only then discuss reasons and trade-offs. Two lists overlapping does not mean the disagreement is only about wording; not overlapping does not mean the goals differ: one may list an item as required by regulation, the other list the same item as required by the budget.

### Four identical parts, one fully reversed order

Line the two writings up: ESTJ is Te–Si–Ne–Fi and INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te. Read INFP's arrangement backwards and you get ESTJ's: dominant and inferior swap, auxiliary and third swap, and no part is missing.

A position describes a theoretical preference in type dynamics, not a scale of ability, not how effortful something feels, and not a sequence of actions. The same person shifts toward the other side when authorised, pressed with questions or asked to sign; under time pressure, ESTJ may hesitate over one detail and INFP may fill in the whole form in one go.

On the third position, ESTJ's Ne and INFP's Si are marked with different attitudes across sources, and some tables give only the function name. This page uses the common marking; when a version disagrees, check which table it cites, then return to the first two positions for this pair. The disagreement does not change the first two and does not explain how early anyone acts. Both full pages are the [ESTJ profile](/en/personality/estj) and the [INFP profile](/en/personality/infp).

Align the conditions first: the same event, the same material requirements, the same deadline, the same post and the same information. If one is the organiser and the other only helping, or one has run five similar events, those conditions will cover both columns.

Each row states the basis each may attend to in the same matter, and the last column names the axis it mainly corresponds to. Both types may use the other's approach; the table records only which is taken first more often, and sequence, speed and whether anything is delayed do not enter the judgement.

| One event, one set of material, one deadline | ESTJ: the basis more likely attended to | INFP: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The same registration requirements and event material | Check which facts the form explicitly requires, and what was submitted last time | Look across the material for the connections, and for other event formats it could support | S/N: checkable facts against possibility; deadline and signing authority are shared conditions |
| The note says only "not clearly described" | Weigh how each revised version meets the same published criteria | Weigh which revised version best serves the people the event is meant for, within the same criteria | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| One day left, two fields short | Agree on a provisional plan for completing both fields by the deadline | Keep several workable completion plans open while both confirm the requirements | Outward stance, leaning J/P |
| Someone says the process is too much trouble | Who carries the responsibility if it is bypassed, and which rule applies if something goes wrong | Who the trouble lands on, and whether bypassing shifts risk onto residents | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| Estimating how many will come | Last year's sign-in count for a similar event, and this year's registration list | What patterns in the same sign-in and registration records might suggest about turnout | Sourcing preference, leaning S/N |
| Both review the same feedback before deciding what to revise | May clarify what the note means by talking it through with the other organiser | May clarify what the same note means through private reflection | E/I: processing identical feedback through interaction or reflection |

The differences in the table are not a scale of ability. An INFP who has run a dozen similar events will have the material ready two weeks early, and an ESTJ taking one on for the first time may bend the process for a favour; the same type in a different post moves both columns.

Scope note: the two passages below are editorial fictions covering communication, the organisation of information and cost arrangements only, not approval outcomes, fire or electrical judgements; such judgements belong to the competent authority and licensed professionals.

Working together, the two easily get stuck when one is already at the office window and the other is still asking whether the thing should be done this way. It is rarely about who is right, but about which kind of information each handles first; writing the two lines separately is more useful than arguing.

### One market: coordinating approvals and working with stallholders

(Fictional scene.) The site is a patch of open ground outside a residential compound, and the organisers have been asked to confirm venue, fire-safety, noise and insurance requirements for this fictional event.

One approach works backwards: which stamp is needed by which date, who goes, missing items flagged in red, contacts saved to speed dial, and a visit in person when something sticks. The other talks to stallholders first: who will come, what they sell, whether anyone depends on this market for a month of groceries, and sets the scale from that.

Each has a blind spot. Focusing only on approvals can leave an event that meets the requirements but attracts few stalls or visitors; intentions alone may reach the day and find the power insufficient and the access route non-compliant.

The division follows experience, authority and willingness, not type: whoever knows the registration process, whoever knows the stallholders, whoever has time this week leads that line, and both lines need someone to sign off. Hard conditions — fire access, the load limit, the noise window — are confirmed with the authority by both together and written into one sheet; what can be adjusted, such as the number of stalls, the length of the performance, whether there is sound, is left to the content side. If neither knows the process, contact the relevant authority together, or ask someone experienced to walk the first round with you.

Once a week, ask whether anything that should not have been changed was changed in order to pass review, and put the answer in the minutes; only then does anyone remember what the original was.

### A shared flat's bills: how to handle a gap in the records

(Fictional scene.) Three flatmates share a flat, and after three months the expense records show a difference of 180 yuan.

One position pulls the transactions first and checks them one by one: who bought what, is there a receipt, how much per head; and proposes a fixed monthly transfer date, with reporting any expense over 50 yuan in the group chat. The other handles the cost of the conversation first: is it worth digging through three months of history for a hundred and something, shall we cover it this time and talk it through, while also remembering how awkward it felt to be audited.

Either position can be raised by anyone and accepted by anyone. Checking only the accounts easily turns living together into an audit; covering only the money leaves a new discrepancy next month and a layer of resentment in whoever pays.

The counterexamples are clear: INFP will propose a spreadsheet the second time it does not add up and get the rule established; ESTJ will say "let it go this time, you helped me move".

One method worth trying: agree on a threshold for recording shared expenses, such as 50 yuan in this example, and write down who carries what below it — absorbed individually, or pooled and split at month end. Without that, a shrinking difference in the records does not show the split is fairer, only that some spending has moved out of the records. After a trial month, review two things together: how much shared spending never entered the accounts, and whether each person feels the split was fair.

sections.body_md:
Do not read drive as dominance. Chasing progress is often because everyone knows it will not happen otherwise, and the same person may not raise their voice at home; conversely, a gentle speaker may not yield an inch on a deadline.

Do not read hesitation as having no view. Hesitation is often checking whether this fits one's own judgement, not waiting for someone else to decide. Once settled, it may be explained clearly or not explained again; how far someone holds depends on how much the matter matters to them, not on four letters.

Nor judge by "can they get things done". Navigating an application process and writing event copy are both skills, and both can be trained; a preference says only which end is cared about first, not what level can be reached.

One more to avoid: do not read "all four axes differ" as "complete opposites". The difference on an axis is one of emphasis, not one side having something the other lacks; both types check facts, consider people, make arrangements and keep room.
sections.title: ESTJ and INFP: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When you keep landing between ESTJ and INFP, check the instrument, version, language and how each axis score is defined, then which kind of situation you were referring to when answering: liaison, approvals, writing or support work may give you different examples to think about. The role alone does not predict which letters a test will return. Record role demands separately from personal preference; circumstances push answers, and one score cannot establish a stable tendency.

Put the practice in ordinary life, with no threshold on occasions: take a few recent matters — a returned application, a shared bill, a weekend plan — and write three lines for each: which information you trusted, which standard you weighed, and whether you settled outward or kept it open. Note also who was responsible, who held authority and how tight the deadline was; without that it is hard to tell which step was preference and which was the post.

If the item bank reports axis scores, look at which of the four sit near the boundary; being near a boundary only means this round did not discriminate clearly on that axis, not that two complete types both hold, and it is not a reason to retest. Without axis scores or scoring notes, do not infer a boundary. These records are for reflection, and there is no need to force out a four-letter result.

items.answer:
No. That sentence presses four axes into one and turns two people into opposites.

Read by the four axes: E/I is whether attention and energy turn outward or inward more often; S/N whether sourcing weighs checkable facts and precedent or pattern and possibility; T/F whether judgement weighs one consistently applicable standard or what it means for specific people; J/P whether an arrangement is formed outward first or room is kept. On the same matter, both may lean to the other side on all four axes, or separate on only one or two; that has to be read across comparable situations, and a single performance does not show it.
items.question: Is the difference really just "one talks process, one talks feelings"?

items.answer:
Because whether two people can work together does not depend on how function labels are arranged. "Exactly reversed" is a description under the common four-function notation used here, not a cause of collaboration going well or badly.

Collaboration depends on clear duties, sufficient authority, shared information and aligned goals. In the same project both types may watch the process, and both may watch whether the thing is worth doing; the division is negotiated by experience and authority, not by function positions. Conversely, two people of the same type collaborating badly need no function arrangement to explain it.
items.question: With the function order fully reversed, how can they still work together?

items.answer:
Both types can chase a process, and both can adjust a plan for a value; a function position does not restrict what anyone can do.

The same behaviour cannot be read backwards into a function position. The same person behaves differently under different duties, authority and information, and later wording cannot identify which position was called on — lines such as "this is not about you" or "next time we follow the process" reflect the situation and relational pressure. What discriminates better is the reason: across comparable situations, do you more often cite "which requirement must be met, who is responsible", or "what this means for the people involved".
items.question: INFP also chases a process, and ESTJ also changes a plan for a feeling — how does that fit?

items.answer:
Not by type, but by experience, authority and willingness.

Both can ask about the hard conditions, and both can set the scale and the content. A workable order asks the hard conditions first — which fields cannot change, who holds approval, when the deadline is — and whoever knows the process goes; then sets scale and content within those conditions, and whoever knows the participants goes. The order can be agreed, but it should follow who knows how and who has time; content first and conditions later tends to mean starting over, and conditions first with no content tends to produce a compliant event nobody wants to attend.
items.question: For an event needing registration, who goes first?

items.answer:
Usually over how clear is clear enough: one feels the accounts must be clear for the friendship to survive, the other feels that counting too carefully is itself what damages it.

A usable method is to state the threshold: what amount gets recorded, how smaller amounts are handled, who keeps the record, and who carries spending below the threshold. Written as one clear line, it is easier to check than an unspoken understanding. After a trial, look together at what never entered the accounts and how fair each person feels the split was; whether arguments decrease can only be known after a review, and cannot be promised in advance.
items.question: Sharing a flat, where do the disagreements over money stick?

items.answer:
Trust neither immediately; check first whether the conditions were comparable: the instrument and version, the language, the situation you answered from, and how each axis score is defined and scored.

If the tool reports an interpretable dividing point, a score near it can mean the letter is sensitive to small changes in your answers; if the tool gives no axis scores or scoring notes, make no boundary inference. More useful is to write one line a week for several weeks — which information you trusted, which standard you weighed, whether you settled or kept it open — and separate role demands from personal preference, without rushing to pin a four-letter result on yourself.
